title: Deep Kernel Hedging
subtitle: arXiv 2609.34474 · options hedging with a learned similarity score

sections.title: The big idea
beats: Goal: protect a position in an option by trading the stock underneath it. That protection is called hedging.
The paper learns a hedging rule from example price paths instead of a textbook formula.
Key tool: a kernel (a score for how similar two situations are). Similar market moments should get similar hedges.
Twist: a tiny neural net first squeezes the market data into a better summary. Then a bell-curve kernel compares those summaries. Together that's a deep kernel.
Result: it hedges better than plain kernels and than deep hedging, mostly when data is scarce.
sections.example: A weather app that says 'today looks like these 5 past days, so bring an umbrella' is using similarity the same way.
sections.sayback: Explain to a friend why 'similar situations get similar hedges' is a useful rule.

quiz.q: What does the neural net add?
quiz.a: It learns a better summary of the market before the similarity is scored.

sections.tieback: Liquid Bot tie-in: theme weights are a crude 'similar setups behave alike' rule. A kernel is the math version.

sections.title: The setup: hedging error
beats: You owe an option payoff Y at the end. You start with some cash and trade the stock on fixed dates.
At each date the rule looks only at what you can see now (price, volatility) and says how many shares to hold.
Self-financing means no money comes in or out. Profit only comes from what you already hold.
Hedging error = what you owe, minus what your cash grew to, minus your trading gains. Zero means perfect cover.
Training goal: make the average error small, plus a penalty that keeps the rule smooth.
sections.example: Like budgeting for a bill due in a month: each week you adjust savings so you land right on the amount.
sections.sayback: Say in one sentence what the hedging error measures.

quiz.q: What does a hedging error of zero mean?
quiz.a: Your trades exactly covered the payoff you owe.
So the rule doesn't memorize noise in the training paths.

sections.title: The shortcut: one weight per path
beats: Searching over every possible rule is impossible. There are infinitely many.
A theorem (the representer theorem) proves the best rule is a weighted mix of one building block per training path.
So you only solve for N numbers, one weight per path.
The weights come from a table Q: entry (i, j) scores how alike path i's trading is to path j's.
With squared error there's a one-line formula for the weights.
sections.example: Instead of writing a new recipe from scratch, you blend your 50 tested recipes in the right amounts.
sections.sayback: Why does turning 'infinite choices' into 'N weights' matter?

quiz.q: What is one entry of Q?
quiz.a: How similar two training paths' trading patterns are.

sections.title: Making it fast: random waves
beats: Problem: Q has N×N entries. With many paths it gets huge and slow.
Fix: random Fourier features. Approximate the bell-curve kernel with D random cosine waves (D = 100 here).
Each path becomes a list of 100 numbers. Now you solve for 100 weights, no matter how many paths you have.
The waves are drawn once and frozen. More waves = closer to the exact answer.
Training uses mini-batches and the Adam optimizer, like any neural net.
sections.example: Describing a song by the strength of 100 notes instead of comparing it to every other song.
sections.sayback: Explain why cost stops exploding as you add more paths.
